# 2. Why Not Simply Pool the Data? {.focus-workflows #why-not-simply-pool}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.lab-layout .round-lab}
::: {.round-panel}
<div class="design-list compact">
<p><strong>Centralized:</strong> pool all patient data in one place. Strongest statistical control; highest legal and logistical movement burden.</p>
<p><strong>Local-only:</strong> each hospital trains and keeps its own model. Easiest governance; weakest generalization beyond one hospital.</p>
<p><strong>Federated:</strong> data stay local; a shared model is built by exchanging model updates instead of records.</p>
</div>
<div class="center-statement compact">Federated learning is one collaboration design among several &mdash; not automatically the right one.</div>
:::
::: {}
<iframe class="lab-frame full live-embed" data-base-src="live/admin/index.html?embed=1" src="live/admin/index.html?embed=1&demo=1" title="Live poll results and design-mapping panel — syncs automatically" scrolling="no"></iframe>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:50. Target 1:50 &middot; skip-if-late: show only the three kickers, skip the center statement.

Thesis: FL is one design in a larger design space, chosen for a reason, not by default.

Opening sentence: "Look at the panel that just appeared on the dashboard. A few of you picked 'send everyone's data to one place and retrain' — that's centralized pooling, and it's a completely reasonable answer in a classroom. In medicine, it's usually the option that's off the table first. Notice something else: nobody picked 'keep every hospital's model fully separate' — because the question assumed we were combining them. That's local-only, and it's on this slide too."

Main evidence: Rieke et al. and Kairouz et al. provide broad FL framing; the fuller five-design taxonomy (including federated evaluation and federated analytics) is in the backup slide if the audience wants the complete map.

Clinical translation: A PhD protocol should justify why model updates need to move, not merely assert that raw data stay local.

Transition: "So what does federation actually look like as a mechanism? One round, start to finish."

Optional skip: Skip to the center statement only if very short on time.

Interaction instructions: The panel on the right is the same live mirror as Slide 1 — point at the real counts and pro/con text there, then use the cards on the left as the clean written recap of the same three designs. Ask who voted to pool the data, and ask one of them what would have to be true institutionally for that to actually work (single IRB, single data-processing agreement, no cross-border transfer restriction). Before moving to Slide 3, switch to the real dashboard tab once (the embedded panel here has no clickable controls) and click "Reveal federation map" — nodes appear immediately, uniformly sized, since everyone who voted has already joined.

Exact citation reminders: Rieke et al. 2020; Kairouz et al. 2021; Karargyris et al. 2023.
:::

## Backup: Five Collaboration Designs

<div class="backup">

:::: {.editorial-two-col .visual-led .workflow-focus}
::: {}
![](assets/diagrams/workflows.svg){.visual .tall fig-alt="Five collaboration designs: central data pooling, local-only modelling, federated learning, federated evaluation, and federated analytics."}
:::
::: {}
<div class="design-list compact">
<p><strong>Pool data:</strong> strongest control, highest movement burden.</p>
<p><strong>Stay local:</strong> easiest governance, weakest generalization.</p>
<p><strong>Federate training:</strong> share updates, not raw records.</p>
<p><strong>Federate evaluation:</strong> test where data live.</p>
<p><strong>Federate analytics:</strong> estimate before modelling.</p>
</div>
:::
::::

The full five-design vocabulary distinguishes federated *training* from federated *evaluation* (test a model where data live, without training) and federated *analytics* (estimate simple statistics before ever fitting a model). Use this slide if the audience asks "isn't there something short of full FL?"

</div>

# 3. One Federated-Learning Round {#one-federated-learning-round}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.lab-layout .round-lab}
::: {.round-panel}
![](assets/diagrams/fl-round.svg){.visual fig-alt="A federated-learning round with local training, update transfer, aggregation, and return of the shared model."}
<p class="callout">Raw patient data stay local. Information still moves.</p>
:::
::: {}
<div class="round-steps">
<div class="step fragment"><span>1</span>Global model exists at the server.</div>
<div class="step fragment"><span>2</span>Server broadcasts it to hospitals.</div>
<div class="step fragment"><span>3</span>Patient data never leave any hospital.</div>
<div class="step fragment"><span>4</span>Each hospital trains locally.</div>
<div class="step fragment"><span>5</span>Only model updates travel back.</div>
<div class="step fragment"><span>6</span>The server aggregates the updates.</div>
<div class="step fragment"><span>7</span>A new shared model is broadcast again.</div>
</div>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:30. Target 1:30 &middot; skip-if-late: click through all 7 steps in silence, skip narration of steps 2-3.

Thesis: One round looks simple; the trouble is hidden inside the word "aggregate."

Opening sentence: "This is the mechanism behind the question I just asked you. Train locally, send an update, aggregate, repeat. Watch step 6 closely — that is where today's activity lives."

Main evidence: FedAvg is the baseline aggregation idea, but site size, label quality, prevalence, and fairness goals can point in different directions. The mechanics here are covered by McMahan et al. 2017.

Clinical translation: If a small hospital serves the population you most care about, sample-size weighting can make it nearly silent — this is exactly what the live activity will let you see happen.

Transition: "Check your phone — still on the welcome screen? Good, hold there one more slide."

Optional skip: If short on time, narrate steps 1, 4, 5, 6, 7 only and skip 2-3.

Interaction instructions: Click through the fragments one at a time, pointing at the diagram for each step.

Exact citation reminders: McMahan et al. 2017; Kairouz et al. 2021.
:::

## Backup: FedAvg Formula

<div class="backup">

FedAvg updates a shared model by a weighted average of local model parameters or updates:

$$
w_{t+1} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{n_k}{\sum_j n_j} w_{t+1}^{(k)}
$$

Where \(n_k\) is the number of local training examples at site \(k\). The formula is easy to teach; the clinical policy embedded in the weights is not.

</div>

# 6. Round 1: Federated Averaging {#round-1-federated-averaging}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.closing-grid}
::: {}
<div class="theory-block">
<p class="theory-formula">F(w) = &sum;<sub>k=1</sub><sup>K</sup> p<sub>k</sub> F<sub>k</sub>(w) &nbsp;&nbsp;with&nbsp;&nbsp; p<sub>k</sub> = n<sub>k</sub> / &sum;<sub>j</sub> n<sub>j</sub></p>
<p class="theory-legend">F<sub>k</sub>(w): what hospital k wants the model to optimize locally. p<sub>k</sub>: how much influence that hospital receives. Aggregation is partly a statement about whose objective matters &mdash; and partly a statistical/optimization choice, not purely a fairness decision.</p>
</div>
:::
::: {}
<div class="live-cta-row">
<a class="live-cta" href="live/admin/index.html?autoqr=1" target="fl-dashboard" rel="noopener">Open Federation Dashboard →</a>
</div>
<p class="live-status-note">Same dashboard tab. Click "Start Round 1" &mdash; the arrows and weight bars appear for the first time.</p>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2:20. Target 2:20 &middot; skip-if-late: show the resultant arrow only, skip clicking through per-client weights.

Thesis: FedAvg makes every training example count equally — which means hospitals do not count equally.

Opening sentence: "Remember your prediction earlier? Run FedAvg now and let's see how close 'weight by how much data it was trained on' actually gets. Watch the arrows on the right: each one is somebody's simulated update. The white arrow is what the server actually keeps."

Main evidence: p_k = n_k / sum(n_j) is exactly the weight shown in the bar chart; the largest bar is the largest hospital in the room. Formula and picture must correspond exactly. McMahan et al. 2017 is the primary citation.

Clinical translation: A rare-population hospital's clinically important signal can visually shrink to a thin, low-opacity line the moment sample-size weighting is applied.

Transition: "Notice something — not everyone's arrow points the same way. Why not?"

Optional skip: Skip deriving the formula symbol-by-symbol; just point at the correspondence between a bar and an arrow's opacity.

Interaction instructions: On the same dashboard tab, click "Start Round 1" — the vector field and weights panel were deliberately empty until this click, so this is the first time arrows and bars appear; confirm aggregation policy is "FedAvg," and narrate the weights panel: "largest client weight: X%." Point at one specific large node's bar and its thick, opaque arrow, then a small node's thin, faint arrow. Briefly connect back to the opening poll: whoever voted "weight by data" predicted exactly this mechanism.

Exact citation reminders: McMahan et al. 2017; Kairouz et al. 2021.
:::

# 7. The Data Are Not IID {#the-data-are-not-iid}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.editorial-two-col}
::: {}
<figure class="iid-compare agree">
<div>
<div class="arrows"><span></span><span></span><span></span></div>
<figcaption>IID-ish: different data, similar learning direction.</figcaption>
</div>
</figure>
<div class="shift-taxonomy compact" style="margin-top:14px">
<div class="shift-card"><div class="shift-glyph feature"></div><strong>Feature shift</strong><p>scanner &middot; protocol</p></div>
<div class="shift-card"><div class="shift-glyph label"></div><strong>Label shift</strong><p>prevalence differs</p></div>
<div class="shift-card"><div class="shift-glyph concept"></div><strong>Concept shift</strong><p>outcome means differently</p></div>
<div class="shift-card"><div class="shift-glyph workflow"></div><strong>Workflow shift</strong><p>referral &middot; annotation</p></div>
</div>
:::
::: {}
<figure class="iid-compare">
<div>
<div class="arrows disagree-set"><span></span><span></span><span></span></div>
<figcaption>Non-IID: local objectives disagree.</figcaption>
</div>
</figure>
<p class="center-statement compact" style="margin-top:14px">Institution is a latent variable. Federation makes that fact harder to ignore.</p>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2:10. Target 2:10 &middot; skip-if-late: skip the four shift-type cards, keep only the two arrow figures and the center statement.

Thesis: Heterogeneity is not noise to average away; it is a clinical clue, and you already saw it in your own federation.

Opening sentence: "Go back to your own site card. Some of your arrows agreed with your neighbours'; some clearly did not. That disagreement has a name: non-IID."

Main evidence: Zech et al. showed site-level generalization failures in chest radiograph models; FedBN and related work target feature shift by keeping selected normalization local.

Clinical translation: The same habit applies to any multicentre study: stratify, visualize, and document why sites differ before blaming "noise."

Transition: "Before we stress-test the federation, a quick map of where these methods sit — the classics and the frontier."

Optional skip: Skip method names (FedBN) if the audience is clinically mixed; keep only the four shift labels.

Interaction instructions: Ask 2-3 students with visibly different archetypes (read from their own phone) to shout out one line from their site card.

Exact citation reminders: Zech et al. 2018; Li et al. 2021 FedBN.
:::

# 8. FL Classics and the 2026 Frontier {#fl-classics-and-the-2026-frontier}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.editorial-two-col}
::: {}
<span class="kicker">Classics &mdash; not interchangeable "averaging options"</span>
<div class="design-list compact">
<p><strong>FedAvg:</strong> the server-aggregation baseline you just ran.</p>
<p><strong>FedProx:</strong> modifies the <em>local</em> objective with a proximal term, not the aggregation rule.</p>
<p><strong>FedBN:</strong> keeps selected normalization parameters local &mdash; targets feature shift.</p>
<p><strong>SCAFFOLD:</strong> uses control variates to reduce client drift.</p>
<p><strong>FedOpt:</strong> a family of server-side optimizers (momentum, adaptive rates).</p>
</div>
:::
::: {}
<span class="kicker">Frontier, 2026</span>
<div class="frontier-grid">
<div class="frontier-card"><strong>Personalized / target-aware</strong>Whose hospital should the model serve?</div>
<div class="frontier-card"><strong>Multimodal / missing-modality</strong>What can be shared when rows differ?</div>
<div class="frontier-card"><strong>Federated evaluation &amp; analytics</strong>Do we even need training, or just testing and estimation?</div>
</div>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:40. Target 1:40 &middot; skip-if-late: name FedProx, FedBN, and SCAFFOLD only, skip FedOpt and the frontier grid.

Thesis: The frontier is not one topic; naming methods correctly matters more than naming many of them.

Opening sentence: "You've now run the one method almost everyone starts with. Two sentences on where the rest of the field sits, because these get misclassified constantly."

Main evidence: FedProx changes local optimization, not the aggregation weighting; FedBN and SCAFFOLD address feature shift and client drift respectively through different mechanisms; FedOpt generalizes the server update rule. None of these is simply "another averaging formula." The full six-area frontier map (personalization, multimodal, foundation models, federated evaluation/analytics, uncertainty/fairness/robustness, governance) is in the backup slide.

Clinical translation: A PhD student can position a project by naming a method's actual mechanism and maturity level, not by treating every name as interchangeable.

Transition: "Let's put one of these ideas under real pressure. Round 2."

Optional skip: Skip to the classics list only; point to backup for the full frontier grid if asked.

Interaction instructions: Ask the audience which frontier area is closest to their own project.

Exact citation reminders: Li et al. 2020 FedProx; Li et al. 2021 FedBN; Karimireddy et al. 2020 SCAFFOLD; Reddi et al. 2021 FedOpt.
:::

:::
::: {.frontier-card}
<strong>Uncertainty, fairness, robustness, drift</strong>
Who is failed by the average?<br>
<span>Essential</span> FeTS + UQ.
:::
::: {.frontier-card}
<strong>Infrastructure, governance, reproducibility</strong>
Who is responsible when it breaks?<br>
<span>Deployment-critical</span> Eden.
:::
::::

**More mature:** FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, SCAFFOLD, FedOpt; secure aggregation, differential privacy, membership-inference vocabulary; medical FL reviews and case studies.

**Clinically urgent:** site-level external evaluation; calibration, subgroup performance, abstention; governance and accountability.

**Emerging:** multimodal missing-modality benchmarks; federated foundation models and PEFT; federated causal inference and analytics at scale.

</div>

# 9. Round 2: Federation Under Stress {#round-2-federation-under-stress}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.closing-grid}
::: {}
<p class="question-band">Predict first: what will happen to the aggregate when one hospital looks very different?</p>
<div class="design-list compact" style="margin-top:10px">
<p><strong>B &middot; Rare hospital:</strong> a small, clinically distinctive site.</p>
<p><strong>C &middot; Suspicious update:</strong> one extreme, unexplained update.</p>
</div>
:::
::: {}
<div class="live-cta-row">
<a class="live-cta" href="live/admin/index.html?autoqr=1" target="fl-dashboard" rel="noopener">Open Federation Dashboard →</a>
</div>
<p class="live-status-note">Same dashboard tab. Click "B &middot; Rare hospital," then compare with "Clipped FedAvg."</p>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2:00. Target 2:00 &middot; skip-if-late: trigger the event, show FedAvg's result, skip the strategy comparison entirely.

Thesis: Robust aggregation bounds an outlier's influence; it cannot diagnose why the outlier happened.

Opening sentence: "Predict before I click: if I make one hospital's population rare and clinically important, what happens to its voice under FedAvg?"

Main evidence: Under FedAvg a small hospital's contribution shrinks toward its sample-size weight regardless of clinical importance; clipping and coordinate-median bound an extreme update's magnitude but do not explain it. Possible real-world causes of an unusual update — label error, preprocessing error, domain shift, corrupted training, a malicious client — are observationally similar from the server's side.

Clinical translation: "If this is the population we most care about, did federation solve our problem?" Robust statistics manage influence, not clinical meaning.

Transition: "So a global number just changed. Did it change for everyone the same way?"

Optional skip: Pick ONE event only — Event B (rare hospital) is the stronger default because it connects directly to the next two slides. Use Event C only if the room specifically wants to discuss data integrity.

Interaction instructions: On the same dashboard tab, ask the room to predict out loud, THEN click "B · Rare hospital." Show FedAvg's result, then click one alternative aggregation policy (Clipped FedAvg or Coordinate median) to compare in under 30 seconds. Do not reveal a root cause if you also run Event C — ask the room to list candidate explanations instead.

Exact citation reminders: Kairouz et al. 2021 (robust aggregation framing); no single paper is cited for the synthetic event itself.
:::

# 10. Did It Help Every Hospital? {#did-it-help-every-hospital}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.editorial-two-col}
::: {}
<figure class="mean-worst-compare">
<div class="stat-tile"><span class="figure">↑ mean</span><span class="caption">Global average performance</span></div>
<div class="stat-tile worst"><span class="figure">↓ worst site</span><span class="caption">Rare / shifted hospital</span></div>
</figure>
<p style="font-size:0.5em;color:var(--grey);margin-top:8px">Numbers come from the live dashboard's synthetic evaluation panel &mdash; a coherent deterministic teaching simulation, not empirical research evidence.</p>
:::
::: {}
<p class="center-statement">The average model does not treat the average hospital.</p>
<p class="callout" style="margin-top:14px">"The average is not the deployment site."</p>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:30. Target 1:30 &middot; skip-if-late: read the two boxed statements only, skip re-opening the dashboard.

Thesis: A clinically acceptable global average can still hide an unacceptable hospital.

Opening sentence: "Look back at the evaluation panel: the mean can go up while the rarest or most shifted hospital goes down at the same time."

Main evidence: This mirrors what FeTS reports in real distributed multi-site evaluation — average performance can hide institutional outlier weaknesses; the synthetic panel here is a teaching projection of that same finding, not a claim about a specific method.

Clinical translation: A study should predefine minimum acceptable performance at the site and subgroup level, not only global AUROC.

Transition: "So the model changed. What actually moved to make that happen — and what didn't?"

Optional skip: If very short, skip straight to the callout line and move on.

Interaction instructions: Point at the dashboard's evaluation panel (still visible from the previous slide) and read the mean and worst-site numbers aloud.

Exact citation reminders: Zenk et al. 2025 FeTS; Karargyris et al. 2023.
:::

# 11. Security: What Moves, What Stays {#privacy-and-security-what-moves-what-stays}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.lab-layout .privacy-lab}
::: {.privacy-map}
<div class="flow-summary">
<p><strong>Stays local:</strong> raw records, direct identifiers, local preprocessing.</p>
<p><strong>Still moves:</strong> model updates, metrics, counts, logs, released models.</p>
</div>
<p class="callout">Federated learning changes the privacy problem. It does not delete it.</p>
:::
::: {}
<p style="font-size:0.6em;color:var(--grey);padding:0 8px">The full interactive threat-surface explorer (gradient leakage, membership inference, poisoning, secure aggregation, differential privacy) is in the course resources.</p>
<a class="live-cta secondary" href="labs/privacy-threat-model/index.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open Privacy Threat-Surface Explorer →</a>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:30. Target 1:30 &middot; skip-if-late: read only the callout line and the two-column list.

Thesis: Privacy depends on flows, actors, logs, releases, and attack models, not only on where raw data sit.

Opening sentence: "Your phone never sent us a single patient record. It sent a two-number summary of an update — and in a real system, that update itself is an information channel."

Main evidence: Gradient leakage, membership inference, poisoning, secure aggregation, and differential privacy each address different parts of the threat surface; none of them is "solved" simply because raw data stayed put.

Clinical translation: Ask for a threat model in plain language: who can see what, what could they infer, and who responds if the assumption breaks.

Transition: "This is exactly the kind of problem real medical federations are already living with. Let's look at scale."

Optional skip: Skip the "open full explorer" pointer if time is tight; it is resource material, not live content.

Interaction instructions: Do not open the full lab live. State the caveat sentence exactly as written — it is the single most important sentence in this section.

Exact citation reminders: Shokri et al. 2017; Zhu et al. 2019; Bonawitz et al. 2017.
:::

# 12. Medical FL in the Real World {#medical-fl-in-the-real-world}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.compact-evidence}
::: {}
<span class="kicker">Scale</span>
Pati et al.: 71 sites, six continents, 6,314 glioblastoma patients trained together.
:::
::: {}
<span class="kicker">Distributed evaluation</span>
FeTS: 41 models evaluated across 32 institutions &mdash; average performance hid site-level failure, exactly like your dashboard just showed.
:::
::: {}
<span class="kicker">Evidence gap</span>
612 healthcare-FL articles reviewed; only 32 (5.2%) were real-life clinical applications (Teo et al. 2024).
:::
::::

::: {.center-statement .compact}
Everything you just simulated becomes harder in real hospitals: more heterogeneity, more governance, less control.
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:30. Target 1:30 &middot; skip-if-late: keep only the scale and evidence-gap stats, drop FeTS detail.

Thesis: Medical FL has real scale and real evidence-of-failure-modes, but limited clinically mature evidence overall.

Opening sentence: "Everything you just did with 60 phones has a real analogue at 71 hospitals across six continents."

Main evidence: Pati et al. 2022 (scale); Zenk et al. 2025 FeTS (distributed evaluation, site-level failure); Teo et al. 2024 (612 articles, 32 real-life applications, 5.2%).

Clinical translation: A clinical PhD should separate technical feasibility, external validation, and routine clinical value when reading this literature.

Transition: "So what should actually stick with you — not just from FL, but from the whole course?"

Optional skip: Skip the Teo et al. evidence-gap statistic first if very short on time; keep scale and FeTS.

Interaction instructions: Ask the audience what kind of evidence would change their local practice. The full governance stack and brain-cancer case detail are in backup slides if there is time for questions.

Exact citation reminders: Pati et al. 2022; Karargyris et al. 2023; Zenk et al. 2025; Teo et al. 2024; Li et al. 2025; Bujotzek et al. 2025.
:::

# 13. Four Lenses to Borrow {#four-lenses-to-borrow}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.borrow-grid}
::: {.borrow-card}
<span>1</span>
<div>
<strong>Bias &mdash; whose data shapes the model.</strong>
Sample-size weighting gives the biggest contributor the most influence by default. That is a policy choice, and it can silence small, clinically important populations.
</div>
:::
::: {.borrow-card}
<span>2</span>
<div>
<strong>Security &mdash; data staying local is a start, not an ending.</strong>
Updates, metrics, counts, and logs are still a channel. Ask what could be inferred from each of them.
</div>
:::
::: {.borrow-card}
<span>3</span>
<div>
<strong>Heterogeneity &mdash; disagreement is signal, not noise.</strong>
Non-IID data is not a bug in the room; it is the room. Stratify and document why sites differ.
</div>
:::
::: {.borrow-card}
<span>4</span>
<div>
<strong>Fairness &mdash; a rising average can hide a falling site.</strong>
Predefine worst-site and subgroup thresholds. The average is not the deployment site.
</div>
:::
::::

::: {.center-statement .compact}
You do not need to run federated learning to use these four habits in your next project.
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2:00. Target 2:00 &middot; skip-if-late: read the four card headlines only, skip the second sentence of each.

Thesis: The most useful takeaway is four transferable habits, not a verdict on whether to use FL.

Opening sentence: "Four lenses. You have already watched every one of them happen on your own phone in the last twenty-some minutes — and every one of them applies even if you never touch FL again."

Main evidence: Bias comes from the FedAvg weighting derivation and the giant-hospital dynamic in Round 1; security from the privacy slide; heterogeneity from the non-IID slide and Round 2; fairness from the worst-site slide. Bias and fairness are deliberately distinct: bias is about who shapes the model, fairness is about who the result then fails.

Clinical translation: These map directly onto grant writing, ethics review, data-processing agreements, analysis plans, and deployment discussions — for any multicentre project, federated or not.

Transition: "One more thing before questions — a small tool to keep exploring these four lenses on your own."

Optional skip: If very short, read cards 1 and 4 only — they are the pair most often conflated.

Interaction instructions: Ask the audience which of the four would change one of their current projects, federated or not.

Exact citation reminders: TRIPOD+AI; DECIDE-AI; Eden et al. 2025.
:::
